abstract: Ultrafast GHz bursts enable laser-matter interactions where successive excitations collectively build sustained nonequilibrium states and efficient material interactions. However, directly generating pulse trains at GHz rates remains challenging. Alternatively, repetition-rate multipliers (RRMs) divide each oscillator pulse into equidistant replicas, but either suffer from dispersion imbalances that prevent simultaneous compression or are limited to few pulses per burst. Here, we introduce dissipative erasure, which first suppresses the differences by spectral filtering and then regenerates the optical bandwidth via nonlinear amplification without restoring the erased differences. We derive two scaling results: as the repetition rate increases geometrically with RRM stages, maximum path differences approach a finite limit; meanwhile, dispersive differences weaken quadratically with filtering. We demonstrate dissipative erasure experimentally, generating 100-$μ$J bursts, comprising thousands of 100-fs pulses at 51.3 GHz, from a Yb-fiber amplifier. Dissipative erasure has diverse potential applications for suppressing deterministic or stochastic differences before recovering desired optical properties.
